analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $17 an hour, indexed to median wage growth after that.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $17 has sat untouched in the House Education and Workforce Committee since April 2025, with 176 of 217 House Democrats cosponsoring and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour in steps over six years, reaching $17 an hour, then raise it every year along with the growth in the median national wage so it stops falling behind prices. It would also phase out the separate, lower minimum wages for tipped workers, newly hired teenagers, and workers with disabilities, eventually paying all of them the full minimum wage. The bill went to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum, including millions of tipped restaurant and service workers who would see their base cash wage climb from $2.13 an hour to the full minimum wage, and workers with disabilities now paid below the minimum under special certificates. Workers earning slightly above the minimum often get raises too as pay scales shift upward.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $9.50 on the effective date, then in annual steps to $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and $17 five years later, and after that raises it each year by the percentage growth in the median hourly wage of all workers [S2].

Phases out the tipped minimum wage: the base cash wage for tipped employees rises in steps from $6.00 to $15.00, then to $17, and one day after that the separate tipped minimum is repealed so tipped workers must be paid the full federal minimum [S2].
Gives employees the legal right to retain their own tips and requires employers to inform them of that right, and makes it a violation for employers to keep or use employee tips [S2].
Phases out the subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20, raising it from $6.00 until it reaches the full minimum, then repealing the separate youth rate [S2].

Raises the subminimum wage allowed for workers with disabilities under section 14(c) certificates in steps from $5.00 to the full minimum wage, bars any new employers from getting these certificates, and sunsets the program entirely once the phase-in reaches the full minimum, while directing the Labor Department to help employers and workers transition to regular competitive employment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay wages at or near the minimum, concentrated in restaurants, hospitality, retail, agriculture, and care work. Some of the cost would likely reach consumers through prices and some could show up as reduced hours. Employers operating sheltered workshops under disability wage certificates would lose the ability to pay subminimum wages and would need to restructure or close.

drawbacks.text: The schedule raises the wage floor substantially over six years for businesses that pay minimum wage, and smaller restaurants and care providers say phased increases of this size force price increases, reduced hours, or closures; the restaurant industry in particular has long opposed eliminating the tipped wage because tips currently cover much of its wage bill.

Some economists argue that a much higher wage floor reduces employment or hours for the least-experienced workers; the bill keeps a temporary lower rate for newly hired teenagers, which acknowledges that concern but only until the separate youth rate is repealed.
The full $17 wage arrives six years after enactment, and workers with disabilities in certificate jobs do not reach the full minimum until year five, so the help is backloaded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: workers earning near $7.25 an hour would see their pay roughly double over six years, and the groups paid least under current law — tipped workers and workers with disabilities — would eventually get the same floor as everyone else. The costs fall on specific employers rather than on taxpayers, and the six-year phase-in gives businesses time to adjust, though the elimination of the tipped wage and of disability subminimum certificates would genuinely disrupt some restaurants and sheltered workshops. On balance the bill is a straightforward wealth transfer from low-wage employers to low-wage workers, with the main honest objection being the risk of job or hour losses at the bottom of the wage scale.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced in April 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Bobby Scott of Virginia, the ranking Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee, introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2025 on April 8, 2025 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which is the only action the bill has received; there have been no further steps in the action history [S4].
176 House Democrats cosponsored the bill — 176 of the 217 House Democrats — and no Republicans are listed as cosponsors [S3].

The bill text phases the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 over six years, indexes it to median wage growth thereafter, and phases out the separate minimum wages for tipped workers, newly hired teens, and workers with disabilities [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers paying the $7.25 federal minimum wage are better off, since the bill has not moved and the current wage floor remains in place. Low-wage workers have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers paying the $7.25 minimum, so far

for.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
for.role: Ranking Democrat, House Education and Workforce Committee; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2025 and gathered 176 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — in the months since it was referred on April 8, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 176 cosponsors is a House Democrat, and no Republican has signed on, so the bill currently has support only from the minority party [S3].

industries.note: Restaurants would have to pay tipped servers a rising base wage reaching the full minimum, replacing the $2.13 tipped cash wage that lets customers' tips substitute for employer pay. Servers would be guaranteed a real wage floor; owners would bear the cost directly.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and employers holding disability wage certificates
industries.note: These employers can currently pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage under special certificates. The bill raises that floor in steps, bans new certificates, and sunsets the program, ending subminimum pay for disabled workers.

industries.industry: Retail, hospitality, agriculture, and other minimum-wage employers
industries.note: Any employer paying at or near $7.25 would face a wage floor rising to $17 over six years, with the option to raise prices or adjust staffing. Workers at the bottom of the pay scale are the direct beneficiaries.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 223 of 435 House seats and controlling the Education and Workforce Committee, a minimum-wage bill with no Republican cosponsors is very unlikely to get a committee markup or a floor vote this Congress. Barring a change in chamber control or a late procedural move, it will probably sit in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
